conceptTag: Write one for a business software tool
readerTitle: The 4 p.m. phone list: writing a promise for a clinic app
caseNote: 가상 사례 (물리치료 클리닉용 예약 알림 앱, 사무실 케이터링 업체) · 수치와 제품은 모두 설명용
insight: 소프트웨어의 가치 제안은 기능 설명이 아니라 고객이 지금 하고 있는 방식보다 무엇이 나아지는지를 고객의 하루 언어로 쓴 약속이다.
misconception: B2B 소프트웨어의 헤드라인은 기능과 기술(AI, 올인원, 플랫폼)을 잘 설명할수록 좋고, 비교 대상은 경쟁 앱이다.

sources.text: 모든 사례와 문구는 설명용 가상 예시
가치 제안, 차선책(next best alternative), 고객 관점의 전환 비용: 이 유닛의 개념 레슨 CUS-02-03, CUS-02-05, CUS-02-06

factChecks.note: 노쇼율, 시간 절감 등 실제 통계는 쓰지 않았습니다. '환자 2,000명', '20명 점심', '15% 절약'은 모두 가상 수치이며 카드에 illustrative 표시가 있습니다.
적용 레슨이라 새 개념을 도입하지 않았습니다. 사용 개념은 CUS-02-03, CUS-02-05, CUS-02-06입니다. relatedLessonIds는 두 개만 허용되어 CUS-02-03과 CUS-02-05를 넣었습니다. 전환 비용(CUS-02-06)도 6번 카드와 정리 카드에 쓰입니다.

cards.title: The receptionist's 4 p.m. phone list
body: At 4 p.m. every day, the receptionist at a small physio clinic starts calling tomorrow's patients. Half the calls go to voicemail. Some patients still don't show up.
A founder has built an app that texts reminders and lets patients rebook in one tap. Her homepage says: *The all-in-one AI-powered patient engagement platform.* Clinic owners visit. Few sign up.

image.label: Receptionist on the phone with a long paper call list
image.brief: 작은 클리닉 접수대. 오후 4시 시계, 접수 직원이 수화기를 들고 긴 종이 명단에 체크 표시 중. 옆 모니터에는 흐릿하게 'All-in-one AI platform'이라고 적힌 웹페이지. 실제 로고나 브랜드는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which headline would you test first?
body: The founder wants one new headline for small clinic owners. Pick the one most likely to make them read on.

options.text: Smart patient engagement for modern clinics
options.feedback: It sounds polished, but any competitor could say it. It names no problem and no result, so it isn't yet a **value proposition**.

options.text: Fewer empty appointment slots, without the 4 p.m. phone calls
options.feedback: It names the customer's problem and what gets better. That's a **value proposition**: a specific promise to a specific customer.

options.text: Trusted by clinics across the country
options.feedback: Proof helps once people know what you do. On its own, it tells a busy owner nothing about their own problem.

cards.title: A promise, not a description.
body: A **value proposition** says who you help, what gets better for them, and why they should pick you.
The old headline described the product: platform, AI, engagement. The new one describes the owner's day: empty slots that cost money, and an hour of calls nobody enjoys.
Owners don't buy reminders. They buy a full diary and a calmer front desk.

image.label: Two headlines compared: product words vs customer outcome
image.brief: 좌우 비교 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 카드 'All-in-one AI platform'(회색, 기능 아이콘들), 오른쪽 카드 'Fewer empty slots, no 4 p.m. calls'(밝은 색, 꽉 찬 예약표와 내려놓은 전화기). 오른쪽을 강조. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Who are you really competing with?
body: To sharpen the promise, the founder must say why it beats the alternative. What is the typical small clinic's real alternative today?

options.text: The two bigger reminder apps on the market
options.feedback: They matter for some buyers. But most small clinics haven't bought any app, so beating rivals doesn't explain why to change at all.

options.text: The receptionist's phone calls and a paper list
options.feedback: That's the **next best alternative**: what the customer does if you don't exist. Your promise has to beat it, not a rival's feature list.
It looks that way from outside, but they already pay for the calls in staff time. Miss the current routine and you miss the cost you can point to.

cards.title: Beat the phone list, not the rival app.
body: Phone calls feel free because the receptionist is already paid. So "saves money" is weak. "Your receptionist gets her afternoons back" is concrete.
The phone list has one real strength: it's familiar. So the promise must be easy to picture. Patients confirm by text, and a cancelled slot is offered to the next patient on the waiting list.
The line becomes: *Fill cancelled slots automatically. Stop the 4 p.m. calls.*

cards.title: Answer the worry they won't say out loud.
body: Even an owner who likes the promise thinks: moving 2,000 patient records, retraining staff, patients confused by new texts.
That's a **switching cost** from the customer's side: the effort and risk of changing, not the price.
So the founder adds one line under the headline: *We import your patient list and set it up with you in one call.* It removes the hidden cost instead of discounting the visible one.

cards.title: A sharp promise has to be true.
body: Specific claims get tested. If clinics still see empty slots, "fewer empty slots" becomes a broken promise. Only promise what most customers will notice in their first few weeks.
A sharp line also narrows who it speaks to. This one is for small clinics, not hospital groups. That's usually a strength early on, but it's a choice you're making.

cards.title: Now it's a catering company.
body: You cater office lunches. You're writing one line for office managers who order food for team meetings. Today most of them collect orders by email and place them on delivery apps. Which line would you lead with?

options.feedback: It describes your food the way every caterer does. It doesn't say why you beat what the office manager does now.

options.text: Lunch for 20, ordered in two minutes, on one invoice
options.feedback: It beats the **next best alternative**, chasing orders and splitting app receipts, and it lowers the **switching cost**: nothing new to learn.
It compares against the right alternative. But many office managers care more about hassle than price, and a number you can't back up is risky.

cards.softwareNote: Notice the same shape as the clinic app: name the routine the customer already has, then promise the specific thing that gets easier.

cards.title: Write the promise from the customer's day, not your product's features.
body: This lesson put three ideas to work:
list: **Value proposition:** who you help and what gets better for them
**Next best alternative:** compare with what they do today, often a spreadsheet, a phone or nothing new
**Switching costs:** name and remove the effort of changing
cards.callout: **Try it today:** write down what your customer did yesterday instead of using you. Rewrite your headline so it beats that.
